lead: A latch stores one bit in a feedback loop. The loop is closed for part of the clock, so the output either follows the input or holds the last value. Two latches in series, driven by opposite clock phases, form a master-slave flip-flop: the register output changes only at a clock edge. Designers use latches inside flip-flops and SRAM cells, and use registers for pipeline state, counters and control. Correct operation depends on setup and hold checks, and on whether the bit is held by a static loop or by dynamic charge.
prereq: You need: Unit 3 for the transmission gate and for the delay of the inverter pair inside the storage loop.

sections.h3: SR latch, gated D latch and transparency

blocks.text: A latch is a bistable circuit: it has two stable states, one for logic 0 and one for logic 1. In a cross-coupled NOR latch, output Q drives one input of the other NOR gate, and Qbar drives the other. Set S=1, R=0 forces Q=1. Set R=1, S=0 forces Q=0. With S=R=0 the loop holds its state. S=R=1 is forbidden: both outputs go to 0, and the final state after release is a race.
A cross-coupled NAND latch works the same way with active-low set and reset. The feedback loop continuously restores the stored level, so this is static storage.

A gated D latch removes the forbidden input. It has data D and enable EN. When EN=1, Q follows D and the latch is transparent. When EN=0, the loop closes and Q holds the last value. A transmission-gate latch uses two TG switches controlled by EN and its complement. One switch admits D; the other closes the inverter-pair feedback. The D latch is level-sensitive, not edge-triggered. It is small, fast and common inside flip-flops and as the storage element of static cells. The 6-transistor SRAM cell achieves the same static storage with cross-coupled inverters and access transistors, not with a gated D latch.

A master-slave D flip-flop uses two D latches in series. The first is the master, the second the slave. Section 1 defined the D latch: it is transparent when its EN input is 1. Drive the master's EN with CLKbar and the slave's EN with CLK, so their transparent phases do not overlap. While CLK=0, the master is transparent and follows D; the slave is opaque and holds the old output. At the rising edge, the master becomes opaque and stores the value at D. The slave becomes transparent and copies the master. The output changes once, at the edge. After that, the master is fixed, so the slave has nothing new to pass. This is why two latches make a rising-edge-triggered register.

Edge triggering matters in synchronous systems. A transparent latch can pass a glitch or a late arrival while enabled; a flip-flop samples only around the edge. A register is n flip-flops in parallel, sharing one clock. Each bit has the same control. An enable input adds a multiplexer or clock gating so Q keeps its value. An asynchronous reset forces Q=0. A shift register connects Q of stage i to D of stage i+1.

Timing defines whether a register-to-register path works. Let the launch flip-flop send data and the capture flip-flop receive it. t_cq is the clock-to-Q delay: the maximum time from the clock edge to a valid Q. t_comb is the combinational logic delay between them. t_su is the setup time: data must be stable this long before the capture edge. t_h is the hold time: data must stay stable this long after the edge. The aperture is the small window around the edge, roughly t_su plus t_h, during which data must not change.

blocks.where: T is the clock period in ns; t_cq is clock-to-Q delay; t_comb,max is the longest combinational delay; t_su is setup time.

blocks.text: Setup is checked on the longest path. Setup slack = T − t_cq − t_comb,max − t_su, and it must be ≥0. Hold is checked on the shortest path.

blocks.where: t_comb,min is the shortest combinational delay between the same registers; t_h is hold time.

blocks.text: Hold slack = t_cq + t_comb,min − t_h, and it must be ≥0. The hold check does not contain T; slowing the clock cannot fix a hold failure. The shortest clock period is T_min = t_cq + t_comb,max + t_su, so f_max = 1 ÷ T_min.

Clock skew is the difference in clock arrival time between the two flip-flops. Define t_skew = capture clock arrival time − launch clock arrival time. Positive t_skew means the capture edge arrives later, which relaxes setup and tightens hold: setup slack = T − t_cq − t_comb,max − t_su + t_skew, and hold slack = t_cq + t_comb,min − t_h − t_skew.

Static storage uses the feedback loop. The loop supplies charge lost by leakage, so the bit survives with the clock stopped or running arbitrarily slowly. Dynamic storage uses charge on a transistor gate capacitance or a wire capacitance. A transmission gate writes the charge; when the gate turns off, no loop restores it. Leakage removes the charge and the node voltage droops. The latch must be refreshed before the droop exceeds the allowed ΔV.

blocks.where: I_leak is leakage current in A; C is storage capacitance in F; ΔV is allowed droop in V; f_min is the minimum refresh frequency in Hz.

blocks.text: A dynamic latch cannot run at DC. A static latch can. Two-phase non-overlapping clocking uses Φ1 and Φ2. The two phases are never high together. This prevents two latches from being transparent at the same time and racing. Only a few universities teach the detail; the rule is enough for most exams.

figure.caption: The clock alternates high and low. The D latch is transparent while CLK is high; the register output changes only for a short time after a rising edge and holds in between.

spec.aria: The latch follows the input whenever the clock is high, while the register output changes only at the clock edges.

examples.question: A register-to-register path has clock-to-Q delay t_cq = 0.3 ns, combinational delay t_comb = 1.2 ns, setup time t_su = 0.15 ns, hold time t_h = 0.10 ns and clock period T = 2 ns. Use the same t_comb for the hold check. (a) Find the setup slack and state whether setup passes. (b) Find the hold margin and state whether hold passes. (c) Find the shortest clock period and the maximum clock frequency.
steps: Setup slack = T − t_cq − t_comb − t_su = 2 − 0.3 − 1.2 − 0.15 = 0.35 ns. This is ≥ 0, so setup passes.
Data arrival for hold = t_cq + t_comb = 0.3 + 1.2 = 1.5 ns. Hold margin = 1.5 − t_h = 1.5 − 0.10 = 1.4 ns. This is ≥ 0, so hold passes.
Shortest clock period T_min = t_cq + t_comb + t_su = 0.3 + 1.2 + 0.15 = 1.65 ns.
Maximum frequency f_max = 1 ÷ T_min = 1 ÷ (1.65 × 10^−9 s) = 606.06 × 10^6 Hz = 606.06 MHz.
examples.answer: Setup slack is 0.35 ns, hold margin is 1.4 ns, the shortest clock period is 1.65 ns, and the maximum clock frequency is 606.06 MHz.
examples.check:
t_cq = 0.3
t_comb = 1.2
t_su = 0.15
t_h = 0.10
T = 2.0
setup_slack = T - t_cq - t_comb - t_su
hold_margin = (t_cq + t_comb) - t_h
t_min = t_cq + t_comb + t_su
f_max_mhz = (1 / t_min) * 1000
print(round(setup_slack, 2))
print(round(hold_margin, 2))
print(round(t_min, 2))
print(round(f_max_mhz, 2))

traps: A single gated D latch is level-sensitive, not edge-triggered. Only the master-slave pair or another edge circuit is a flip-flop.
Setup uses the longest path and contains T; hold uses the shortest path and has no T. Slowing the clock fixes setup, not hold.
Swapping the clock phases in a master-slave latch changes the active edge and can create a race if the two phases overlap.
A dynamic latch has a minimum clock frequency; a static latch works down to DC. Do not give a dynamic latch a maximum-frequency-only answer.
Mixing t_su and t_h signs in slack formulas is the most common numeric slip. Write data-arrival minus required-arrival for each check.

quiz.q: Define setup time t_su and hold time t_h for a flip-flop.
quiz.a: t_su is the time data must be stable before the capturing clock edge. t_h is the time data must remain stable after the edge.

quiz.q: Why is a gated D latch not called edge-triggered?
quiz.a: It is transparent for the whole enable level. While EN=1, any D change reaches Q; it does not sample only at an edge.

quiz.q: A path has t_cq = 0.25 ns, t_comb,max = 0.90 ns, t_su = 0.10 ns and T = 1.50 ns. Find the setup slack.
quiz.a: Setup slack = 1.50 − 0.25 − 0.90 − 0.10 = 0.25 ns. It is ≥ 0, so setup passes.

quiz.q: A hold check fails on a short path. Can you fix it by lowering the clock frequency? Explain.
quiz.a: No. Hold compares data arrival after the edge with t_h; T cancels out. Add delay in the short path, increase t_cq, or reduce t_h.

quiz.q: Why does a master-slave pair of latches give edge-triggered behavior?
quiz.a: The master and slave are transparent in opposite phases. The output takes the sampled master value only when the slave opens, once per clock period.

quiz.q: State one difference between static and dynamic storage in a latch.
quiz.a: Static storage uses a feedback loop that restores charge continuously. Dynamic storage uses charge on a capacitance and needs refresh before leakage causes too much droop.

quiz.q: A dynamic latch has C = 20 fF, leakage I_leak = 2 nA and allowed droop ΔV = 0.10 V. Find the minimum clock frequency.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry uses pulsed latches and time borrowing to relax setup on critical paths, and sense-amplifier flip-flops in high-speed links. Clock gating and retiming decide where registers sit in a real pipeline. Dynamic storage appears in DRAM and in some low-power caches, where refresh and retention are first-order design constraints. Search next for pulsed latch, time borrowing, clock skew and retention voltage.
